new.title: Meet the Flemish Primitives in the Groeningemuseum
new.desc: Bruges was where Jan van Eyck and Hans Memling painted in the 15th century, and the Groeningemuseum holds the city's own collection of their jewel-like panels. The detail in the fabrics and faces still looks unreal up close.
new.tip: Go straight to the Van Eyck room first while it is quiet, then work your way through the later centuries.

new.title: See Memling's paintings in the old hospital
new.desc: Sint-Janshospitaal is one of the oldest surviving hospital buildings in Europe, and its medieval wards now hold a set of Hans Memling paintings made for the very place they hang in. The museum also tells the story of centuries of care and healing.
new.tip: Do not miss the old apothecary at the back, a pharmacy that looks as if it closed yesterday.

new.title: Look up in the Gothic Hall of the City Hall
new.desc: The City Hall on the Burg, begun in 1376, is one of the oldest in the Low Countries and the city council still meets here. Upstairs, the Gothic Hall has a painted, vaulted wooden ceiling and wall paintings of the city's history.
new.tip: Stand in the middle of the hall and tilt your head back; the hanging vault keys are the real show.

new.title: Slip into the courtyard of an almshouse
new.desc: Behind small doors all over the city hide godshuizen: rows of whitewashed cottages around a garden, built from the 14th century onward for the elderly poor and still lived in today. The Rooms Convent and Spanoghe almshouses are along Katelijnestraat.
new.tip: People live here, so keep your voice down and stay on the garden paths. If a gate is closed, try another; some only open now and then.

new.title: See what is on at BRUSK, the new art hall
new.desc: Opened in 2026 in the heart of the museum district, BRUSK is Bruges' new hall for big temporary exhibitions of old, modern and contemporary art. The dark green building by Robbrecht en Daem frames views of the Belfort and the church towers around it.
new.tip: On the first Friday of the month it stays open late. Bar Brusk downstairs is open to everyone, ticket or not.

new.title: Find the bronze skull on the Smedenpoort
new.desc: The Smedenpoort is one of the four medieval city gates still standing. On its wall hangs a bronze skull, a copy of the head of a man who tried to let French troops into the city through this gate in 1691 and was executed for it.
new.tip: The skull is on the city side of the gate. From there, follow the green ramparts north or south for a quiet walk.

new.title: Visit Guido Gezelle at the Centrale Begraafplaats
new.desc: Opened in 1787 when burials inside the city were banned, Bruges' central cemetery in Assebroek is full of sculpted tombs of poets, artists and politicians, among them the beloved Flemish priest-poet Guido Gezelle. Locals compare it to Père Lachaise.
new.tip: It is especially atmospheric on a misty autumn day. It is a short bike ride from the Gentpoort.

new.title: Visit the 600-year-old archers' guild
new.desc: On Carmersstraat, the Schuttersgilde Sint-Sebastiaan has been shooting bows since the 14th century. The guild house holds portraits, silver and archives, and members still shoot at tall vertical targets in the garden. Charles II of England was an honorary member during his exile.
new.tip: Visits are by appointment only and mostly for groups; email the guild ahead. Otherwise, look for the slim tower from the street.

new.title: Ask for advice at 't Brugs Beertje
new.desc: This small brown café on Kemelstraat is the city's reference beer bar, with a list of around three hundred Belgian beers. The staff are known for matching a beer to your taste.
new.tip: It is closed on Wednesdays and fills up fast in the evening; come early and tell them what you usually like.

new.title: Drink a Trappist in a vaulted cellar
new.desc: Le Trappiste on Kuipersstraat pours its beers under the brick vaults of an old cellar, with a long tap list leaning towards Trappist and abbey beers.
new.tip: Ask for the rotating guest taps; they often have small Belgian brewers you will not find elsewhere.

new.title: Watch the match with locals at 't Hof van Beroep
new.desc: On Langestraat, far from the tourist squares, 't Hof van Beroep is a traditional Flemish pub where Bruggelingen come to talk football over a beer. One drink easily becomes an evening.
new.tip: Go when Club Brugge or Cercle Brugge are playing for the full atmosphere.

new.title: Dare a strange praline at The Chocolate Line
new.desc: Chocolatier Dominique Persoone made his name with daring flavour combinations, and his shop on Simon Stevinplein is a temple of creative chocolate art.
new.tip: Pick at least one praline with a flavour you would never put in chocolate yourself.
new.q: The Chocolate Line Simon Stevinplein 19 Brugge

new.title: Eat with the neighbours at Tom's Diner
new.desc: Tucked into a quiet street in the Sint-Gillis district, Tom's Diner is a relaxed bistro with a rock 'n' roll feel, popular with locals for its honest cooking and shareable plates.
new.tip: Book ahead; it is small and the regulars know it. Walk back via the Langerei.

new.title: Go down into 't Poatersgat
new.desc: Behind an easy-to-miss door on Vlamingstraat, steps lead down into a candlelit cellar bar with medieval stone walls. Its name means 'the monks' hole'.
new.tip: Look for the small entrance in the wall; it is easy to walk straight past it.

new.title: Take the first canal boat of the day
new.desc: Bruges was built around its reien (canals), and from the water you see gardens, back walls and low bridges that you will never find on foot. The guides tell the stories in several languages.
new.tip: Boats cannot be booked online; queue at a landing stage near the Rozenhoedkaai right at opening time to beat the crowds.

new.title: Follow the forgotten Augustijnenrei
new.desc: Dug in the 12th century, the Augustijnenrei is one of the least known canals in the centre, lined with old merchant houses and crossed by the Augustijnenbrug, one of the city's oldest bridges.
new.tip: Continue to the Gouden-Handrei and the Spiegelrei for a loop that tourist boats skip.

new.title: Stroll the Coupure like a local
new.desc: The Coupure is a canal dug through the city to link it to Gent and Oostende. Today it is a calm stretch of water with houseboats and trees, where Bruggelingen walk their dogs.
new.tip: Start at the Kruisvest end and walk south towards the Gentpoort; there are benches along the water.

new.title: Explore the Concertgebouw Circuit
new.desc: The red-brick Concertgebouw on 't Zand is the city's modern landmark, with famously good acoustics. During the day the Concertgebouw Circuit lets you wander backstage and past its sound art installations.
new.tip: Finish with a drink at the Concertgebouw Café, or check the programme for an evening concert.

new.title: Taste new brews at the Bruges Beer Festival
new.desc: Every year since 2007, a local club of beer lovers has gathered dozens of brewers and hundreds of beers for two days, often with premieres of brand-new beers and live music.
new.tip: Get your tasting glass and tokens early and start with the lighter beers. Check the website for this year's date.

new.title: Skate at Wintergloed in Koning Albert I-park
new.desc: From late November until the end of January, Bruges turns into Wintergloed (Winter Glow): an ice rink and winter bar in Koning Albert I-park, Christmas markets in the centre and a makers' market in the city halls.
new.tip: Skate in the late afternoon, then walk to the Markt when the lights come on.

new.title: Wander the white village of Lissewege
new.desc: Lissewege, part of Bruges since 1971, is a polder village of whitewashed houses along a little canal, dominated by a stubby 13th-century church tower. Nearby stands the huge medieval barn of the former Ter Doest abbey.
new.tip: Climb the church tower for a view over the polders to Bruges, then walk to the Ter Doest barn. The train from Brugge stops in Lissewege.

new.title: Walk the Atlantic Wall bunkers at Raversyde
new.desc: Just west of Oostende, a whole network of German bunkers, gun batteries and trenches from both world wars lies preserved in the dunes. It is one of the best-kept stretches of the Atlantikwall.
new.tip: Allow a couple of hours and wear sturdy shoes. The coast tram stops at Raversyde.

new.title: Walk the Dodengang trench near Diksmuide
new.desc: On the bank of the IJzer, the Dodengang (Trench of Death) is a preserved Belgian trench where the enemy lines were only metres away for four years. It was one of the first memorial sites opened after the war.
new.tip: Combine it with the IJzertoren a few kilometres upriver; cycling along the IJzer between them is easy.

new.title: Stand before the Grieving Parents in Vladslo
new.desc: In the German military cemetery at Vladslo near Diksmuide kneel Käthe Kollwitz's two stone figures, the Grieving Parents. Her own son Peter lies buried in front of them.
new.tip: It is a quiet place in the woods; come by bike from Diksmuide and give yourself time there.

new.title: Visit Kortrijk's Begijnhof and the Broeltorens
new.desc: Kortrijk's UNESCO-listed beguinage, founded in 1238, is a tiny walled world of 17th-century houses where the last beguine in the world lived until 2013. A few steps away, the two Broeltorens guard the river Leie.
new.tip: Look for the statue of Marcella Pattyn, the last beguine, then cross the Leie for the best view of the towers.

new.title: See the Halletoren on Tielt's market square
new.desc: Tielt's belfry rises out of the old cloth hall in the middle of the Markt and belongs to the UNESCO-listed belfries of Belgium and France. Around the town, walking and cycling routes pass old windmills.
new.tip: Tielt is on the train line between Brugge and Kortrijk, so it is an easy stop on the way.

new.title: Walk out on the Blankenberge pier
new.desc: Blankenberge's pier, with its Art Deco touches from 1933, reaches about 350 metres into the North Sea. Rebuilt after the First World War, it is now a protected monument.
new.tip: Walk to the very end at sunset for the widest sea view on this stretch of coast.

new.title: Step into Talbot House in Poperinge
new.desc: In 1915 two army chaplains opened this town house as 'Every Man's Club', a place where soldiers of any rank could rest behind the front. Its rooms, garden and attic chapel still feel lived in.
new.tip: Visit the Hopmuseum further along the same street, and the old death cells in the town hall courtyard.

new.title: Admire the Grote Markt of Veurne
new.desc: Veurne's main square is one of the most complete in Flanders, lined with Renaissance gables of yellow brick, the Landhuis with its UNESCO belfry and the Sint-Walburgakerk just behind.
new.tip: On the last Sunday of July the hooded penitents of the Boetprocessie carry crosses through these streets.

new.title: Taste hopscheuten in Poperinge
new.desc: Poperinge is Belgium's hop capital, and in early spring its restaurants serve hopscheuten, the young white shoots of the hop plant, often with a poached egg and a creamy sauce. They are only picked for a few weeks.
new.tip: Ask for them in the restaurants around the Grote Markt in March; the Hopmuseum explains the rest of the hop story.

new.title: Drink an Abt 12 at St.Bernardus in Watou
new.desc: In the hop fields of Watou, the St.Bernardus brewery makes its famous abbey beers next to the fields where its hops grow. The brewery has a tasting room, tours and a guesthouse.
new.tip: Cycle here through the Hoppeland around Poperinge; you must be 18 or older to enter the site.

new.title: Try a sour red Rodenbach in Roeselare
new.desc: Roeselare's Rodenbach brewery is famous for its Flemish red-brown ales, matured for years in huge oak vats. The tart, wine-like beer is unlike anything else in Belgium.
new.tip: Check the brewery's website for visits, or order one in a café on the Grote Markt. KOERS, the cycling museum, is in the same town.

new.title: Join the Sunday tour at De Dolle Brouwers
new.desc: In the village of Esen near Diksmuide, 'the mad brewers' have made their cult beers in an old brewery since 1980, starting with the dark Oerbier. The tour ends with tastings straight from the cask.
new.tip: The English tour is on Sunday afternoon; the Oerbar tasting bar is open at weekends.

new.title: Have cake at Tante Marie in Damme
new.desc: On Damme's main street near the church, Tante Marie is a cosy café known for its homemade cakes and coffee, the perfect reward after cycling along the canal from Bruges.
new.tip: On the second Sunday of the month there is a book market on Damme's Markt; time your visit for it.

new.title: Buy fish straight off the boat in Nieuwpoort
new.desc: At Nieuwpoort's fish market, the catch of the local boats is sold every morning from Monday to Saturday. It is a real working harbour, far from the beach promenades.
new.tip: Go early in the morning. Afterwards, look out over the Ganzepoot locks from the King Albert I monument.

new.title: Watch the shrimp fishers on horseback at Oostduinkerke
new.desc: Oostduinkerke is the only place in the world where shrimp are still caught on horseback: heavy Brabant horses wade chest-deep into the surf pulling nets, as fishermen did along the whole North Sea coast.
new.tip: They go out around low tide, mostly in the warmer months; check the Koksijde tourist office for the schedule, and visit the NAVIGO fishery museum nearby.

new.title: Get lost in the Westhoek dunes of De Panne
new.desc: At Belgium's westernmost tip, the Westhoek nature reserve is a sea of wild, shifting sand dunes where you cannot see a single building. It feels more like a desert than the Belgian coast.
new.tip: Climbing the loose sand is harder than it looks; bring water and follow the marked paths. The coast tram ends in De Panne.

new.title: Walk the Vauban ramparts of Ieper
new.desc: Ieper is still ringed by star-shaped ramparts designed by Vauban, now a green belt with bomb-proof casemates and the small Ramparts Cemetery by the Rijselpoort.
new.tip: Walk from the Menenpoort to the Rijselpoort in the hour before the Last Post at eight.

new.title: Catch a cat at Ieper's Kattenstoet
new.desc: Every three years Ieper holds its Cat Parade, with giant cats and floats, ending with a jester throwing toy cats from the belfry into the crowd and a mock witch burning on the Grote Markt. The next one is on 9 May 2027.
new.tip: Stand in front of the Lakenhalle (Cloth Hall) if you want a chance to catch a cat.

new.title: Climb the IJzertoren in Diksmuide
new.desc: The 84-metre IJzertoren is a peace memorial with a museum on war, peace and Flemish history spread over its floors. From the top you look out over the IJzer front and the flat polders.
new.tip: Take the lift up and walk down through the museum floors. Pass under the Paxpoort on the way in.
